resources.title: Business formulae
resources.summary: All fourteen formulae in the Business specification, which lists them under twelve headings, for costs and revenue, break-even, cash flow, profit and margins, loans and investment, each worked through with numbers.
resources.statusNote: The specification says: "Formulae will not be provided in the examinations for Paper 1 or Paper 2." So learn every one, and write the formula down before you put the numbers in.

items.name: Total costs
items.symbols: TC is total cost, TFC total fixed costs and TVC total variable costs. Fixed costs £2000, plus £3 a unit for 500 units: $2000 + 1500 = £3500$

items.name: Break-even point in units
items.symbols: Sales price and variable cost are for one unit. $\dfrac{2000}{8 - 3} = 400$ units. Each unit sold brings in £5 more than it costs to make, so 400 units cover the £2000.

items.name: Break-even point in costs or revenue
items.symbols: $400 \times £8 = £3200$. At break-even the costs are the same: $2000 + 400 \times 3 = £3200$.

items.name: Margin of safety
items.symbols: $500 - 400 = 100$ units: sales could fall by 100 before a loss

items.name: Opening balance
items.formula: $\text{opening balance} = \text{closing balance of the previous period}$
items.symbols: Last month closed at £300, so this month opens at £300

items.name: Closing balance
items.symbols: $£300 + £800 = £1100$, which is next month's opening balance

items.name: Gross profit
items.symbols: Cost of sales is what it cost to make or buy the goods that were sold. $£4000 - £1500 = £2500$

items.name: Gross profit margin
items.symbols: $\dfrac{2500}{4000} \times 100 = 62.5\%$: 62.5p of every £1 of sales is gross profit

items.name: Net profit
items.symbols: Other operating expenses are the running costs, such as rent, wages and advertising. $£2500 - £2000 = £500$

items.name: Average rate of return
items.symbols: A £10 000 machine earns a total profit of £6000 over 3 years. Average annual profit is $6000 \div 3 = £2000$, so the return is $\dfrac{2000}{10\,000} \times 100 = 20\%$ a year.

applications.title: Pricing a school fair stall
applications.body: A cake stall pays £40 for the pitch and £0.50 a cake, and sells cakes at £1.50. It breaks even at $40 \div (1.50 - 0.50) = 40$ cakes. Each cake sold after that adds £1 of profit.

applications.title: Choosing a loan
applications.body: A bank lends £5000 and asks for £5750 back in total. The interest is $\dfrac{750}{5000} \times 100 = 15\%$ of the loan. This is the interest over the whole loan, not for each year, so use it to compare loans that last the same time.
